newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean students turn their backs on Pyongyang.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean students turn their backs on Pyongyang.

text.p: Tired of molotov cocktails, teargas and a military-style management, South Korean students are turning their backs on a pro-Pyongyang campus body.
Images of starving North Korean children have also shaken the faith of young revolutionaries in a communist utopia across the border.

Highlighting the changes, Seoul's Yonsei University -- where some of the worst campus violence ever left two teaching blocks gutted and a policeman dead last year -- has elected a devout Christian to head the student body.
Under the leadership of Han Dong-soo, 25, students have abandoned the class struggle and are focusing on issues such as tuition fees and teaching quality.
Students leaders gather each morning for prayers -- and are trying to close down the many bars and nightclubs that surround the campus.
"We're not against rallies, we just want them to be peaceful," Han said.
The shift is being reflected at a growing number of South Korean institutions of higher learning.
Twenty eight universities have severed links with the pro-Pyongyang Hanchongryun, South Korea's most militant student group, which once boasted control over 205 universities.

One former student activist -- a pamphleteer for North Korea's brand of communism known as Juche -- said the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe shattered his beliefs, and Pyongyang's own descent into famine was having a similar effect on the current generation of students.
"Hard core students in the movement won't denounce Pyongyang openly, but I feel the turbulence they are going through," he said.
Students who oppose Hanchongryun say they are tired of being treated as foot soldiers in the movement.

"Times have changed. But those running Hanchongryun are still living in the past," said Han Ji-ham, a student representative at Korea University, referring to the role that massive student demonstrations played in toppling previous military-backed governments.
A small cadre of leaders set Hanchongryun policies in secret meetings where important information is communicated via hand signals because of fears about police wiretaps.
At demonstrations, leaders direct the chanting and signal when to hurl rocks, advance on police lines, and retreat.

Documents, books and videos on North Korea are discreetly circulated to indoctrinate members, and "patriots" are chosen to be sent to the North. Those who return from visits to Pyongyang are hailed as heroes.
Although Yonsei's Han expressed admiration for his predecessors who fought for democracy, he said today's students have a new role to play.
"We should focus on issues closer to home, such as reforming our school and the student culture," he said.
Han was elected after riots at Yonsei last August were crushed in a military-style assault by tens of thousands of riot police backed by helicopters.

Hanchongryun is not altogether a spent force. A national corruption scandal involving aides to President Kim Young-sam and dozens of politicians, combined with a sinking economy, are fuelling student anger.

Yoo Dong-yul, a specialist at the state-run Strategic Institute for Counter North Korea, said Hanchongryun's could try to make a comeback by orchestrating a surge of violence during annual spring demonstrations this month.
